finding.claim: iconUrl is stored with no validation and later fetched server-side by the nightly sync job, so a user can make the server issue GET requests to arbitrary hosts, including internal addresses and cloud metadata endpoints such as http://169.254.169.254/. The response bytes are read.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of PUT /profile, passed to Profile.update(webhook, icon)

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives the attacker-controlled icon string
this.iconUrl = icon is stored with no check of scheme, host or IP; only the webhook argument is validated
sync() builds URI.create(iconUrl) and issues the GET from the server's network position

finding.guards_checked: The regex at line 12 covers only `webhook`, not `icon`. There is no scheme or host allowlist, no private-IP check, and no DNS pinning for iconUrl. The webhookUrl path is not vulnerable: matches() is a full-string match against the fixed host https://hooks.example.com/ followed by 20 alphanumerics, so it cannot be redirected to another host. HttpClient does not follow redirects by default.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the unvalidated `icon` (the regex at line 12 only checks `webhook`), and src/Profile.java:23 issues a GET to URI.create(iconUrl) and reads the bytes, so no closing guard exists; the code does not show whether PUT /profile is low-privilege, but this is the user-supplied update() argument.
